REASONS
FOR DECISION

A.

Introduction
and Overview

[
1
]

D.M. and J.K. are involved in matrimonial proceedings under the
Divorce
Act
[1]

and the

Family Law Act
[2]

They have two children of their marriage: S.K., age 15 and C.K., age 14.

[
2
]

D.M. and J.K are also involved in child protection proceedings under the

Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017
.
[3]
The Society
had been involved with the family for several years because of concerns
regarding D.M.’s, the mother's mental health. The children were removed from
the care of their mother and brought to a place of safety (their father’s J.K’s
home) on February 1, 2019. The children have resided with their father since
their removal to a place of safety.

[
3
]

On February 6th, 2019, Justice Parfett made a temporary without
prejudice order placing the children under the care of their father subject to
the terms of a temporary supervision order, with access to their mother at the
discretion of the Society and in accordance with the children's wishes. The Office
of the Children's Lawyer was ordered to provide independent legal counsel to
both children. Justice Parfett’s order was extended.

[
4
]

On April 8th, 2019, Justice Macleod made a final order finding the
children in need of protection, pursuant to
s.74
of the
Child, Youth and
Family Services Act, 2017
. He also ordered that the children remain with
their father under the terms of a supervision order for a term of four months.
Justice MacLeod granted a restraining order against D.M.

[
5
]

For what follows, it shall be necessary to keep in mind that the Society
did not seek what used to be called a Crown wardship; it sought a custody
order. J.K. consented to the Society’s motion. And J.K. brought a motion of his
own. J.K. sought an order that D.M. be restrained from approaching and
communicating with the children. Both orders were granted by Justice MacLeod
Under the Act, the court’s orders were subject to a status review hearing. For
the review, the Society brought a motion for a summary judgment. On December
11, 2020, on the review hearing of the custody and restraining orders, Justice
Fraser granted the Society and J.K. a summary judgment for the relief they
respectively requested.

[
6
]

In other words, twenty months after Justice MacLeod’s orders, on
December 11, 2020, on a status review application, Justice Fraser concluded
that the children continued to be in need of protection and granted summary
judgment ordering that the children be placed in custody of their father pursuant
to
s. 102
of the
Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017
, with the
ancillary relief of a restraining order and an access order, with access in the
discretion of J.K.  The Ontario Children’s Lawyer representing the children, supported
the order as being in the best interests of the children and consistent with
their views and preferences. This is the order which is the subject of this
appeal.

[
7
]

D.M. has appealed the summary judgment, and she brings a motion to admit
further evidence on the appeal . In the end, D.M. relies on 7,864 pages of
further evidence for the purposes of her appeal. The evidentiary and legal
(factums and casebooks) record for the motion and the appeal comprised 9,589
pages.

[
8
]

For the reasons that follow, subject to a major qualification, D.M.’s motion
to admit further evidence is allowed. Her appeal, however, is dismissed.

[
9
]

Based on both the original evidence and also on the further evidence,
Justice Fraser made no errors of fact, errors of mixed fact and law, or errors
of law in granting summary judgment to the Society and J.K. pursuant to the

Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017
. Justice Fraser’s reasons for
decision were adequate and the reasons do not provide grounds for an appeal. There
were no procedural errors that would provide grounds to set aside the summary
judgment.

[
10
]

Based on the evidentiary record of further evidence that D.M. wanted
presented, an informed person would not conclude that any of Justices Audet,
Engleking, Parfett, de Souza, Shelton, MacLeod, Smith, MacEachern, Hackland, and
Gomery, whose orders are only tangentially involved in this appeal were biased.

[
11
]

Based on the evidentiary record that D.M. wanted presented to this
court, an informed person would not conclude that Justice Fraser, whose
judgment is under appeal, was biased.

[
12
]

Therefore, D.M.’s appeal must be dismissed.

[
13
]

The heartbreakingly sad truth is that although D.M. loves her children
and although D.M. formerly had the capacity to be an excellent caring parent of
them, she is a victim of her mental health problems, and, unfortunately, the
children are in need of protection when they reside with her.

[
14
]

D.M. believes that her mental health problems have been misdiagnosed and
that she has been the victim of J.K.’s psychological abuse. However, the sad
truth remains that when residing with D.M. - whatever the cause or label of D.M’s
mental health problems may be - the children are in need of protection.

[
15
]

The message for D.M. - from the Society, the Children’s lawyer, the
children, and from this court - is that D.M. should get treatment for her mental
health problems. Then, her relationship with her children might be restored in
the context of the ongoing matrimonial law proceedings. With treatment, there
may yet be a happy ending to this up-until-now sad story.

B.

Methodology

[
16
]

Pursuant to amendments to the
Divorce Act
, which came into effect
on March 1, 2021, “custody” and “access” terminology has been replaced by terms
such as “decision-making responsibility” and “parenting time.
Section 35.4
of
the
Divorce Act
deems a person who had custody of a child by virtue of a
custody order to have parenting time and decision-making responsibility and a
spouse or former spouse who had access by virtue of a custody order to be a person
to whom parenting time has been allocated. The events in the immediate case
occurred before the amendments to the
Divorce Act
came into effect. For
the purpose of these Reasons for Decision, I shall, with a few exceptions, use
the historical terminology.

[
17
]

D.M. raises ten grounds of appeal. These grounds of appeal can be
grouped into three categories; namely: (a) seven due process and jurisdictional
issues, including her allegations of bias by the judiciary; (b) evidentiary
issues; and (c) two substantive legal issues.

[
18
]

There are many due process and jurisdictional issues, but the preeminent
ground of appeal concerns whether the Society’s and J.K.’s cases were
appropriate for a summary judgment. The evidentiary ground of appeal concerns
whether Justice Fraser erred in her findings about D.M.’s mental health problems
and her parenting behaviour. There are several substantive law grounds of
appeal, but the most significant of these concerns the constitutional law paramountcy
doctrine and whether there is a distribution of legislative authority conflict
between
Ontario’s
Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017
and the
federal government’s
Divorce Act
.

[
19
]

The methodology of these Reasons for Decision is to first set out the
legal background for the Society’s summary judgment motion  Second, I shall address,
D.M.’s motion to admit further evidence for the appeal. As already noted, in my
opinion, D.M. is successful on her motion for further evidence for the appeal. Third,
after the scope of the evidentiary record is determined, I shall next describe
the factual background to Justice Fraser’s decision. Fourth, I shall set out
the standard of appellate review. Fifth, I will analyze and discuss D.M.’s
grounds of appeal. Sixth, and finally, I shall address the matter of costs. I
foreshadow to say that in my opinion there should be no order as to costs.

C.

The Legal
Beacon of this Case

[
20
]

This is a child protection proceeding under the
Child, Youth and
Family Services Act, 2017
, and although D.M. raises numerous grounds of
appeal, what is of paramount importance in addressing all of her grounds of
appeal is to always keep in mind that the legal beacon in the immediate case is
the best interests of  S.K. and C.K. While the interests of the parent are not
ignored, the primary focus of attention is on the child not on the parent. Child
protection proceedings are ultimately and fundamentally about what is in the
best interests of the children and not about the plight of the parents.
[4]

[
21
]

For the purposes of the summary judgment motion and for this appeal, the
pertinent sections of the
Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017

are

sections 74
,
81
,
88
,
93
,
101
-
106
,
113
,
114
,
121
, and
137
, which are set out in Schedule
“A” to these Reasons for Decision.

[
22
]

There are usually two major adjudications to be made in a child
protection proceeding. The first matter to be decided, which is the predicate
for the second determination, is whether the child is in need of protection. A
child may be in need of protection for many reasons as set out in
s. 74(1)
of
the
Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017
.

[
23
]

If the child is in need of protection, then the second major adjudication
is that of determining how the child should be protected. The
Child, Youth
and Family Services Act, 2017
provides for seven main types of remedial
order; namely: (a) a supervision order, where the child is placed in the
custody of a parent or other person subject to the society’s supervision for a
period between three to not more than twelve months (
s. 101 (1)
para. 1); (b)
an interim care order, where the society assumes care and custody for not more
than twelve months (s. 101 (1) para. 2); (c) an extended care order, which was
formerly known as a crown wardship (s. 101 (1) para. 3); (d) consecutive orders
of interim society care and supervision (s. 101 (1) para. 1); (e) a custody
order, where custody is granted to a person with the consent of the person (
s.
102 (1)
; (f) a restraining order; (
s. 102 (3)
and
s. 137
); and (g) an access
order, which authorizes contact with the child (
s. 104
-
106
).

[
24
]

The remedial orders made in the immediate child protection proceeding were:
(a) a supervision order; (b) a restraining order; (c) a custody order; and (d) an
access order.

[
25
]

The remedial orders are subject to a status review. The decision under
appeal was a summary judgment decision made for a status review hearing. A
status review is a two-step process. First, the court determines whether the
child continues to be in need of protection and, whether the court should make
an order to protect the child. Second, if it is determined that the child is
still in need of protection, the court must determine what remedial order is in
the best interests of the child.
[5]

In determining what order is required to meet the child’s best interests, the
court must consider from the child’s perspective the degree to which the risk
that prompted the original order still exists and how that risk can be
ameliorated or eliminated.
[6]

[
26
]

In the immediate case, as described in detail below, Justice MacLeod
found the children to be in need of protection and at the status review
hearing,
Justice Fraser concluded that the children
continued to be in need of protection. Justice Fraser granted a summary judgment
making a remedial custody order, with the ancillary relief of a restraining
order and an access order, with access in the discretion of J.K.

[
27
]

Determining access may be an aspect of a child protection order. Access
can come in many forms, including the exchange of gifts, emails, video chats,
photographs, or phone calls, and the form and frequency of access should be
tailored to the child's specific needs and age-appropriate wishes of the child.
[7]

[
28
]

In child protection proceedings, if the court makes an access order it
cannot delegate discretionary decisions with respect to the type, frequency,
and duration of the access to a non-judicial actor because this offends the
principle against self-delegation; it is for the court to impose terms and
conditions of access, and an access order must include at least minimum terms
of access.
[8]

In the discussion below, I shall explain why this principle was not offended in
the immediate case, where D.M.’s access to her children will ultimately be
determined in the matrimonial proceedings which have been stayed but which will
resume once the child protection proceedings are completed.

D.

Summary
of the Child Protection Proceedings in the Immediate Case

[
29
]

By way of a summary of the child protection proceedings in the immediate
case, with the details to be described in the facts portion of these Reasons
for Decision, the major events of the proceedings were:

a.

On February 1, 2019, pursuant to ss. 81 (7) and (8) of the
Child,
Youth and Family Services Act
, with the assistance of the police, a child
protection worker of the Society  brought S.K. and C.K. to a place of safety
(J.K.’s home).

b.

Section 88 of the Act provides that when a child is brought to a place
of safety under s. 81, the matter should be brought before the court for a child
protection hearing under s. 90 (1), and on February 6, 2019, Justice Parfett
made a temporary without prejudice order pursuant to s. 101 of the Act placing
the children under the care of J.K. and under the supervision of the Society.

c.

On February 29, 2019, in the child protection proceeding, Justice de
Souza orders that Justice Parfett’s order continue. Justice De Souza also makes
a restraining and supervised access order against D.M.

d.

On April 8, 2019, the Society’s motion for a custody order and a
restraining order comes on for a hearing before Justice MacLeod, who orders
that: (a) pursuant to
s. 101
of the
Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017
,
the children shall remain with J.K. under the terms of a supervision order for
a term of four months; (b) that pursuant to s.137 of the Act
,
D.M. be
restrained in access or contact with the children; and (c) pursuant to s. 113
of the Act, there be a status review by August 6, 2019.

e.

On August 6th, 2019, there is the first appearance on the Society’s
status review application. The notice of application sets a timetable for the
status review in the child protection proceeding. Child protection cases are
governed by the timetable set out in
Rule 33
of the
Family Law Rules
. In
its Application, the Society seeks a Final Order placing the children in the
custody of the father pursuant to
s.102
of the
Child, Youth and Family
Services Act, 2017

(a custody order).

f.

Almost a year passes before a schedule is set for the hearing of the
status review application. On August 28, 2020, in the child protection
proceedings, Justice Engelking grants the Society leave to bring a summary
judgment motion. The summary judgment motion is scheduled for November 10,
2020. As a backstop, a trial is scheduled for September 2021.

g.

J.K. brings a motion for relief in the summary judgment motion as does
D.M.

h.

The summary judgment motion is heard on November 10, 2020, and on
December 11, 2020, Justice Fraser grants the Society and J.K. a summary
judgment. Justice Fraser dismisses D.M.’s countermotion. The trial date is
vacated as unnecessary. There are no genuine issues requiring a trial and the
child protection proceeding comes to an end with a summary judgment.

i.

On January 8, 2021, pursuant to
s. 121
of the
Child, Youth and Family
Services Act,
2017, D.M. appeals to the Divisional Court.

E.

The
Admission of Further Evidence for the Appeal

1.

Background to the D.M.’s Further Evidence Motion

[
30
]

Before setting out the facts, it is necessary to address D.M.’s motion
for the admission of further evidence for the purpose of her appeal.

[
31
]

The discussion of D.M.’s motion for further evidence may begin by noting
how D.M.’s motion material came to be before this appellate court. In this
regard, the following should be noted:

a.

After D.M. appealed the judgment of Justice Fraser, on March 17th, 2021,
at a case management conference in the Divisional Court, D.M. indicated that
she intended to file further evidence for the appeal.

b.

At the conference, Justice Corbett ordered that it would be up to the panel
hearing the appeal to determine whether there would be further evidence.

c.

For the purposes of perfecting the appeal, Justice Corbett directed D.M.
to file her documents in three categories; namely: (a) category 1, materials
that were before Justice Fraser; (b) category 2, transcripts of evidence or
argument from the summary judgment motion; and (c) category 3, any other
materials that D.M. proposed to rely on for the appeal.

d.

D.M. served the Society, the Children’s lawyer, and J.K. with her appeal
documents and with her motion record and her documents for her motion to admit
further evidence for the appeals.

e.

However, D.M. had difficulty uploading the documents in a timely way to
ontariocourts.caselines.com. At the commencement of the argument of the appeal,
it was revealed that although the parties had been served with all of D.M’s
documents, not all of the documents that D.M. intended to rely on had been
uploaded to ontariocourts.caselines.com. The parties but not the court had the
further evidence.

f.

In these circumstances, the Divisional Court panel recessed the hearing
for an hour, during which the balance of D.M.’s documents (some 5,130 pages of
materials, 1.5 gigabytes) were uploaded. In the end, D.M. relies on 7,864 pages
of further evidence for the purposes of her appeal.

g.

The evidentiary and legal (factums and casebooks) record for the motion
and the appeal comprised 9,589 pages.

2.

Discussion and Analysis of the Request to File Further Evidence.

[
32
]

The discussion of D.M.’s motion to file further evidence may continue by
noting the numerous and diverse nature of the documents that D.M. relies on for
the purposes of her appeal. An examination of these documents reveals that:

a.

Some of the documents are redundant and were before Justice Fraser.

b.

Some of the documents were in existence and could have been before
Justice Fraser, but the documents were not put into evidence.

c.

Many of the documents are copies of materials that are in the court’s
file for the matrimonial proceedings or in the court file for the child
protection proceedings.

d.

Some of the documents are not evidence but are documents setting out
legal, medical, and factual arguments.

e.

Some of the documents are not admissible evidence on a diverse variety
of grounds. Visualize: (a) some of the documents are double or triple hearsay;
(b) some of the documents are expert evidence without a qualified expert or without
compliance with the procedural rules associated with expert evidence; and (b)
some of the documents are inadmissible oath helping.

f.

Some of the documents would not have been admissible because they are
privileged lawyer and client communications or litigation privilege documents,
but advertently or inadvertently, D.M. waived the privilege by disclosing and
relying on the communications.

g.

Some of the documents are immaterial or not relevant or they have marginal
materiality or relevance.

[
33
]

Some of the documents proffered by D.M. are helpful to her case;
however, although she may not appreciate it, she has also proffered abundant evidence
harmful to her case.

[
34
]

The documents submitted by D.M. contain admissions against her interest.
Had D.M. had better counsel than her own counsel, she would not have sought to
introduce the documents as part of her own case. Ironically, documents helpful
to the respondents were introduced by D.M.

[
35
]

I foreshadow to say that admitting the corpus of documents that D.M.
relies on confirms the soundness of Justice Fraser’s decision rather than
undermining it.

[
36
]

Much like the situation in
Windsor-Essex Children's Aid Society v.
E.W
.,
[9]

where the Court of Appeal was prepared to admit all the further evidence, in the
immediate case, the evidence does not change the result and, indeed, as I shall
explain below, the further evidence rather confirms that Justice Fraser made no
errors of fact finding.

[
37
]

With this background to the further documents, the explanation may begin
for my decision,  which is that subject to a major qualification, D.M.’s motion
to admit further evidence should be granted.

[
38
]

Section 134(4)(b) of the
Courts of Justice Act
,
[10]
empowers an
appellate court to admit further evidence for the purposes of an appeal.
Section 134(4)(b) states:

134 (4) Unless otherwise provided, a court
to which an appeal is taken may, in a proper case,

[…].

(b) receive further evidence by affidavit,
transcript of oral examination, oral examination before the court or in such
other manner as the court directs; and

[...]

to enable the court to determine the appeal.

[
39
]

Pursuant to
rule 38 (29)
of the
Family Law Rules
,
[11]
a motion to
admit further evidence on appeal may be brought under s. 134(4)(b) of the
Courts
of Justice Act
.

[
40
]

Pursuant to
s. 121 (6)
of the
Child, Youth and Family Services Act,
2017
, in an appeal in  child protection proceeding, the court may receive
further evidence relating to events after the appealed decision.

[
41
]

The general test for the admission of further or fresh evidence for an
appeal was established in the criminal law case of
R. v. Palmer
.
[12]
The general
test has been adopted and applied in civil law and child protection cases. The
test has four criteria; namely: (a) the evidence should not be admitted if by
due diligence it could have been adduced at the hearing; (b) the evidence must
be relevant, in the sense that it bears upon a decisive or potentially decisive
issue in the appeal; (c) the evidence must be credible, in the sense that it is
reasonably capable of belief; and, (d) the evidence must be such that, if
believed, it could reasonably, when taken with the other evidence adduced at
the hearing, be expected to have affected the outcome.

[
42
]

However, given that the best interests and the welfare of a child(ren)
will be at stake, there is a more flexible test for the admission of further
evidence in custody and children in need of protection cases.
[13]
In child
protection cases, the general test for the admission of further evidence is
more flexible, less technical, and liberal. This flexibility in admitting
further evidence for child protection proceedings is to provide the appellate
court with current information about the condition, means, needs, and
circumstances of the child(ren), but the liberality is not for the purpose of
providing an opportunity for the parties to continue an affidavit war or to
facilitate ongoing litigation between the parents.
[14]

[
43
]

Applying this law to the diverse documents in this case, leads to the
conclusion that D.M.’s motion to admit her extensive corpus of further evidence
should be granted. Although given the diverse nature of D.M.’s further
evidence, it is not possible to make a categorical omnibus decision about
D.M.’s set of documents, some of the documents would satisfy the liberal test
for the admission of further evidence for a child protection appeal. Further, some
of the material filed as further evidence could properly be before the court as
submissions in a factum or in a book of authorities. Other documents are
admissible in the interests of justice and to provide D.M. with the opportunity
she submits she did not have to put forward her best case at the hearing before
Justice Fraser.

[
44
]

However, although all the further evidence should be admitted, it should
be admitted only in accordance with the law of evidence. In this last regard,
it should be noted that in
Kawartha Haliburton Children’s Aid Society v. M.W
..

[15]
the Court of
Appeal held that in child protection proceedings, the court on a summary
judgment motion must conduct a careful screening of the evidence to eliminate
inadmissible evidence, and the court should not give weight to evidence that
would be inadmissible at trial.

[
45
]

Thus, in the immediate case, for the documents that are admissible in
accordance with the laws of evidence, D.M. has been given the benefit of the
doubt about: (a) whether the documents could have been produced at the summary
judgment motion with due diligence; (b) whether the documents are credible; (c)
whether the documents might be relevant; and (d) whether the documents might be
expected to have affected the outcome.

[
46
]

She has not been given the benefit of the doubt about the weight to be
given and the use to be made of the documents. Giving the documents the
evidentiary weight they deserve, all of the further evidence is admitted for
the purposes of her appeal.

F.

Facts

1.

The Tragically Sad Story

[
47
]

The following account of the facts is taken from: (a) the evidence that
was proffered for the summary judgment motion; and (b) the further evidence that
is properly admissible for the purpose of D.M.’s appeal.

[
48
]

Because of D.M.’s concerns that her story be heard and that she should

G.

Standard
of Appellate Review

[168]

D.M.
appeals a summary judgment of a status review in a child protection proceeding under
the
Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017
.

[169]

The
determination of custody and access (now “parenting orders”) are inherently
discretionary decisions involving issues of mixed fact and law and intervention
on appeal is warranted only where there is a material error, a serious
misapprehension of the evidence, or an error of law.
[18]

[170]

In
child protection cases, appellate courts owe a high degree of deference to the
trial judge’s decision and on issues of credibility, a trial judge is uniquely
well placed to make the necessary findings and  apart from exceptional
situations, an appellate court should refrain from interfering with those
findings.
[19]

[171]

Where
a ground of appeal raises an issue of law alone, the standard of review is
correctness.
[20]

[172]

Where
the ground of appeal raises a question of fact, the appellate court must pay
substantial deference to it. Before it may properly interfere, the appellate
court
must conclude that the submitted error
amounts to a “palpable and overriding error”.

The word “palpable” means
“clear to the mind or plain to see”
[21]
, and
“overriding” means “determinative”
[22]

in the sense that the error “affected the result”.
[23]
The Supreme
Court has held that other formulations capture the same meaning as “palpable
error”: “clearly wrong”, “unreasonable” or “unsupported by the evidence”.
[24]

[173]

Examples of palpable error include: (a) findings
made in the complete absence
of
evidence (this could also amount to an error in law); (b) findings
made
in conflict with accepted evidence; (c) findings based on a misapprehension of
the evidence; (d) findings of fact, drawn from primary facts, that are a result
of speculation rather than inference; and (e) findings of fact based on
evidence that has no evidentiary value because it has been rejected by the
trier of fact.
[25]

[174]

Matters
of mixed fact and law lie along a spectrum; where the error of the
decision-maker can be traced to a clear error in principle, it may be
characterized as an error of law and subjected to a standard of correctness;
where the legal principle is not readily extricable, then the matter is subject
to standard of palpable and overriding error.
[26]

H.

Process
and Jurisdictional Grounds of Appeal

1.

Is the Case Appropriate for a Summary Judgment
against a Self-represented Litigant?

[175]

The most substantial and important of D.M.’s process and
jurisdictional grounds of appeal is her submission that the case was not
appropriate for a summary judgment. I will address this ground of appeal before
considering the other process and jurisdictional grounds of appeal.

[176]

Summary
judgment motions are governed by
Rule 16
of the
Family Law Rules
.
[27]
Rule 16 is
para
materia
with Rule 20 of the
Rules of Civil Procedure
.
[28]

Rule
16 states:

RULE 16: SUMMARY JUDGMENT

When available

16. (1) After the respondent has served an
answer or after the time for serving an answer has expired, a party may make a
motion for summary judgment for a final order without a trial on all or part of
any claim made or any defence presented in the case.

Available in any case except divorce

(2)  A motion for summary judgment under
subrule (1) may be made in any case (including a child protection case) that
does not include a divorce claim.

[…]

Evidence required

(4) The party making the motion shall serve
an affidavit or other evidence that sets out specific facts showing that there
is no genuine issue requiring a trial.

Evidence of responding party

(4.1) In response to the affidavit or other
evidence served by the party making the motion, the party responding to the
motion may not rest on mere allegations or denials but shall set out, in an
affidavit or other evidence, specific facts showing that there is a genuine
issue for trial.

Evidence not from personal knowledge

(5)  If a party’s evidence is not from a
person who has personal knowledge of the facts in dispute, the court may draw
conclusions unfavourable to the party.

No genuine issue for trial

(6)  If there is no genuine issue requiring
a trial of a claim or defence, the court shall make a final order accordingly.

Powers

(6.1) In determining whether there is a
genuine issue requiring a trial, the court shall consider the evidence
submitted by the parties, and the court may exercise any of the following
powers for the purpose, unless it is in the interest of justice for such powers
to be exercised only at a trial:

1. Weighing the evidence.

2. Evaluating the credibility of a
deponent.

3. Drawing any reasonable inference from
the evidence.

[…]

[177]

In

Hryniak v. Mauldin
[29]

and
Bruno Appliance and Furniture, Inc. v. Hryniak
,
[30]
the Supreme
Court of Canada held that on a motion for summary judgment, the court should
first determine if there is a genuine issue requiring trial based only on the
evidence in the motion record, without using the fact-finding powers provided
by the rule. The analysis of whether there is a genuine issue requiring a trial
should be done by reviewing the factual record and granting a summary judgment
if there is sufficient evidence to fairly and justly adjudicate the dispute and
a summary judgment would be a timely, affordable, and proportionate procedure.

[178]

If,
however, there appears to be a genuine issue requiring a trial, then the court
should determine if the need for a trial can be avoided by using the powers
under the rule. As a matter of discretion, the motions judge may use those
powers, provided that their use is not against the interest of justice. Their
use will not be against the interest of justice if their use will lead to a
fair and just result and will serve the goals of timeliness, affordability, and
proportionality in light of the litigation as a whole. To grant summary
judgment, on a review of the record, the motions judge must be of the view that
sufficient evidence has been presented on all relevant points to allow him or
her to draw the inferences necessary to make dispositive findings and to fairly
and justly adjudicate the issues in the case.
[31]

[179]

If
a judge is going to decide a matter summarily, then he or she must have
confidence that he or she can reach a fair and just determination without a
trial; this will be the case when the summary judgment process: (a) allows the judge to make the necessary findings of fact; (b) allows the judge to apply the law to the facts; and (c) is a proportionate, more expeditious and less expensive
means to achieve a just result.
[32]

The motions judge is required to assess whether the attributes of the trial
process are necessary to enable him or her to make a fair and just
determination.
[33]

[180]

In

Kawartha Haliburton Children’s Aid Society v. M.W
.,
[34]
the Ontario
Court of Appeal held that summary judgments are jurisdictionally possible in
child protection proceedings; however, determining whether there is a genuine
issue requiring a trial the court must exercise caution and apply the
objectives of the
Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017
including
the best interests of the child. The highly cautious approach to summary
judgment in child protection cases is warranted because of the serious
interests at stake and because the
Charter
rights of parents and
children (security of the person) are implicated in child protection cases.
[35]

[181]

On
a summary judgment motion in a child protection proceeding, even if the
respondent's evidence does not establish a genuine issue for trial because the
evidence is absent or deficient, the court must still be satisfied on the
evidence before it that the Children’s Society has established that there is no
genuine issue requiring a trial.
[36]

[182]

Applying
the cautious approach directed by the Court of Appeal in
Kawartha Haliburton
Children’s Aid Society v. M.W
, summary judgments have been upheld or made
by the Court of Appeal.
[37]

[183]

In

Kawartha Haliburton Children’s Aid Society v. M.W
.,

the Court of Appeal held that in child
protection proceedings, the court on a summary judgment motion must conduct a careful
screening of the evidence to eliminate inadmissible evidence, and the court
should not give weight to evidence that would be inadmissible at trial.
[38]
The opposing
parties affidavits in the court file for the proceeding may be admissible,
trial worthy evidence, as admissions, which is an exception to the rule against
hearsay.
[39]

[184]

Further,
in
Kawartha Haliburton Children’s Aid Society v. M.W
,
the Court of
Appeal held that the court must provide assistance to self-represented
litigants in accordance with the principles set out in the
Statement of
Principles on Self-represented Litigants and Accused Persons
[40]

established by the Canadian Judicial Council. These principles include the
following: (a) access to justice for self-represented persons requires all aspects
of the court process to be, as much as possible, open, transparent, clearly
defined, simple, convenient and accommodating; (b) judges and court
administrators should do whatever is possible to provide a fair and impartial
process and prevent an unfair disadvantage to self-represented persons; and (c)
judges should ensure that procedural and evidentiary rules are not used to
unjustly hinder the legal interests of self-represented persons.

[185]

On
a summary judgment motion, the responding party may not rest on mere
allegations or denials but shall set out, in an affidavit or other evidence,
specific facts showing that there is a genuine issue for trial. The responding
party in a child protection proceeding may rely on affidavits he or she has
already filed and it is not necessary to repeat evidence that he or she has already
given by affidavit in the same proceedings.
[41]

[186]

The
responding party must put their best foot forward on the motion. The judge is
entitled to assume that the parties have put before her or him all of the
evidence that they would be able to adduce at trial.
[42]
The
responding party’s speculation as to possible evidence or elaboration on points
that could potentially be available for trial is not a sufficient response to a
summary judgment motion.
[43]

[187]

Justice
Fraser’s reasons demonstrate a proper application of the principles discussed
in
Kawartha Haliburton Children’s Aid Society v. M.W
. for granting a
summary judgment. In my opinion, the case before Justice Fraser, was, and even
more so the case now before this court, is an appropriate case for a summary
judgment.

[188]

Justice
Fraser was patently aware of the jurisdictional principles, and there was ample
admissible evidence that demonstrated to her and that demonstrate to me that

continuing to be in need of protection and that a custody and restraining order

[189]

There

[191]

There
is no substance to D.M.’s suggestion that she was not appropriately treated as

[192]

On
August 28, 2021, at the Assignment Court for the child protection matter, D.M. told

[193]

If

[194]

There

2.

Ineffective Assistance of Counsel and whether D.M. was a “Special
Party”

[196]

Keeping
in mind that D.M. represented herself at the hearing of the summary judgment
motion, D.M. relies on the alleged ineffectiveness of G.S. and C.N. as her
lawyers of record in the child protection proceedings leading up to the summary
judgment motion as a ground of appeal to have Justice Fraser’s decision set
aside.

[197]

While
I shall address this ground of appeal on its merits, I begin by noting that the
case law establishes that ineffective assistance of counsel cannot be raised as
a ground of appeal unless the criticized counsel is given notice and given an
opportunity to participate in the appeal to dispute the allegation of
professional incompetence.
[44]

Notice was not given in the immediate case, and thus for this reason alone,
this ground of appeal fails.

[198]

As
I shall next explain, in any event, this ground of appeal fails on its merits.

[199]

In
the immediate case, the issue of whether there was ineffective assistance of
counsel is an extraordinarily complex matter because it is entangled with the
issue of whether D.M. was capable of giving instructions to counsel.  In this
regard, it needs to be kept in mind from the factual background that: (a)  D.M.
was self-represented at the outset of the child protection proceeding and then
intermittently represented by G.S. and C.N.; (b) as noted in the description of
the facts, the Society indicated an intention to bring a motion to have D.M.
declared a “special party;” and (c) in the criminal proceedings, there were
psychiatric assessments as to whether D.M. was “NCR” (not criminally
responsible).

[200]

The
matter of whether D.M. was a special party is relevant to her ineffective
assistance of counsel ground of appeal because if she was not a special party,
then she was a competent self-represented litigant for the greater part of the
child protection proceedings, and this circumstance substantially undermines
her argument that the ineffective assistance of G.S. and C.N. much mattered in
the immediate case.

[201]

D.M.
herself strongly disputes that she is a special party. Both G.S. and C.N. were
of the view that D.M. was competent to give them instructions and that she
should not lose her right to give instructions by the appointment of the
Official Guardian and Trustee.

[202]

A
special party under
rule 2 (1)
of the
Family Law Rules
is defined to
include a party who is or appears to be mentally incapable under the
Substitute
Decisions Act, 1992
[45]

in respect of an issue in the case and who, as a result, requires legal
representation. There has never been a motion or a finding that D.M. is a
special party, and there was no obligation on Justice Fraser to assess D.M.’s
mental health as a preliminary matter to the summary judgment motion.
[46]

[203]

The
test for whether a litigant is a special party is a functionality test as to
whether the party is mentally incapable: (a) to understand information that is
relevant to making a decision regarding the issue in his or case; (b) or is not
able to appreciate the reasonably foreseeable consequences of a decision or
lack of a decision about the issues in his or her case, and thus lacks the ability
to instruct counsel.
[47]

[204]

On
this appeal there was nothing to suggest that in the proceedings before the
appeal that D.M. was a special party apart from how the topic emerged in the
facts of the immediate case in the run up to the summary judgment motion. Further
on this appeal, D.M. made a competent oral and written argument. On the appeal,
there was nothing to suggest that D.M. was a special party.

[205]

Thus,
as a factual matter, given her own substantial role as advocate, it is at least
quite difficult for D.M. to point the finger of blame for the outcome of the
summary judgment motion at the lawyers who were removed from the record before
the summary judgment motion was argued.

[206]

Assuming,

test drew on the principles set forth in the Court of Appeal’s decision in

and a strong presumption that counsel's conduct fell within the wide range of

the result in the sense that there is a reasonable possibility that the judge's

4.

Reasonable Apprehension of Bias

[215]

D.M.
advances as a ground of appeal the allegation that there is a reasonable
apprehension of bias. This allegation is advanced against Justice Fraser, but
expressly or implicitly, D.M. makes allegations of a reasonable apprehension of
bias against Justices Audet, Engleking, Parfett, de Souza, Shelton, MacLeod,

[216]

The test for a reasonable apprehension of bias was set out by
Justice de Grandpré in his dissenting judgment in
Committee for Justice and
Liberty v. National Energy Board
.
[54]

The test was approved and adopted by the Supreme Court of Canada in
R. v.
Valente

[55]
and
in
R. v. S.(R.D.).
[56]

The test is whether an informed person, viewing the matter realistically and
practically and having thought the matter through, would think that it is more
likely than not that the decision-maker consciously or unconsciously would not
decide the matter fairly.
[57]

The information of this hypothetical observer would include knowledge of the
traditions of integrity and impartiality of the judiciary.
[58]

[217]

The determination of whether there was a reasonable apprehension of bias requires a
fact-specific inquiry and the record must be assessed in its totality from the
perspective of a reasonable observer who attended the whole hearing.
[59]
In
determining whether a judge’s presumption of impartiality has been displaced,
his or her individual comments or conduct during the hearing of a matter should
not be considered in isolation but within the context of the entire
proceedings.
[60]

[218]

There is a strong presumption that judges dispense justice without bias.
[61]
The grounds
for an apprehension of bias must be substantial,
[62]
but each
case must be evaluated in its own particular circumstances and in light of the
whole proceeding.
[63]

The party alleging bias has the onus of proving it and the threshold of proof
is a high one.
[64]

[219]

The appellate court may examine the oral and written words of the trial judge for
signs he or she prejudged substantive issues or issues of credibility
[65]
or unduly
interfered with the examination of witness and descended into the adversaries’
arena.
[66]

Viewing the judge’s acts individually or cumulatively, the appellate court may
decide that there was a reasonable apprehension of bias and thus a new hearing
is necessary.

[220]

In
the immediate case, I have had the advantage of reviewing the transcripts of
many of the hearings.

[221]

In
my view, in the immediate case, nothing in the several judges’ handling of the
child protection proceedings or the matrimonial proceedings supports a claim of
reasonable apprehension of bias, assessed from the perspective of a reasonable
observer present throughout the proceedings or otherwise compromised the
fairness of the child protection proceedings.

[222]

D.M.’s
lack of success cannot be attributed to any bias by the judiciary. There is no
merit to the ground of appeal.

5.

Adequacy of Reasons

[223]

D.M.
raises as a ground of appeal to have the summary judgment set aside, the
argument that Justice Fraser’s reasons for decision were inadequate.

[224]

Written reasons show the parties that the court has paid attention to their
arguments and treated them fairly and with due process. Providing reasons for a
decision removes the appearance of arbitrariness, makes the process
transparent, and makes the decision-maker accountable because he or she is called
on to explain and justify the decision.

[225]

The question of the adequacy of reasons for decision is whether the reasons, viewed
in light of the record and counsel’s submissions on the live issues presented
by the case, explain why the decision was reached, by establishing a logical
connection between the evidence and the law on the one hand, and the decision
on the other.
[67]

[226]

Inadequate reasons may be a ground of appeal because a trial judge must provide
adequate reasons to account to the parties and to the public for the decision.
[68]
Appellate
intervention based on inadequacy of reasons is justifiable when the inadequacy
prejudices the appellant’s exercise of his or her right to appeal or impedes or
prevents an appellate court from understanding the basis of the decision.
[69]

[227]

To
provide for a meaningful right of appeal, in reasons for decision, judges must
identify the key issues; find the facts relevant to the issues; assess
credibility and reliability where there is conflict; set out the chain of
reasoning; make the decision; and then write the reasons to clearly communicate
the decision.
[70]

[228]

Reasons
should provide the basis for a meaningful consideration of the merits of an
appeal and for meaningful appellate review of the correctness of the decision,
but reasons will be sufficient if they are responsive to the case’s live issues
and the parties’ key arguments and their sufficiency should be measured not in
the abstract, but as they respond to the substance of what was in issue.
[71]
The critical
question is whether in the context of the record, the issues and the
submissions of the parties, the judgment is sufficiently intelligible to show
that the judge understood the substance of the matter and addressed the
necessary and critical issues.
[72]

[229]

An
appellate court must review the record to determine whether the decision can be
rendered more comprehensible when read in the context of the record; however, where
the judge’s reasons is not apparent from the reasoning or the record, the
appellate court ought not to substitute its own analysis.
[73]
The
appellate court will usually decline to provide adequate reasons and salvage
the trial result when the trial judge’s decision turns on instances of
conflicting evidence, evaluations of credibility and reliability, or exercises
of discretion that are properly within the purview of a trial judge.
[74]

[230]

The
mere failure to refer to a piece of evidence does not mean that the judge
failed to consider the matter, and a party must point to something in the
record to justify the conclusion that the judge failed to consider evidence.
[75]
Where
credibility plays an important role in the trial, a trial judge’s failure to
provide an explanation for rejecting the evidence of a key witness may preclude
effective appellate review and compel the court to order a new trial.
[76]

[231]

There is no obligation on a trial judge to record every argument or aspect of the
deliberation process.
[77]

However, for meaningful appellate review, the decision of the court must, at a
minimum, provide some insight into how the legal conclusion was reached and
what facts were relied upon in reaching that conclusion.
[78]

[232]

In
the immediate case, Justice Fraser’s reasons surpass the test for the adequacy
of reasons. A review of the reasons reveals that she correctly informed herself
about the applicable law for summary judgments in the context of a status
review hearing in child protection proceedings. The reasons and the reasoning
was transparent and exposed Justice Fraser’s decision to scrutiny on appellate
review.

[233]

As
discussed above and below, Justice Fraser made no reviewable error in her fact
finding or with respect to the substantive law for a status review
determination. D.M. was informed of why she was unsuccessful and of the factual
and legal findings that led to that outcome.

[234]

This
ground of appeal fails.

Rules

7.

The Refusal to Adjourn the Summary Judgment Motion

[239]

D.M. raises as a procedural and due process ground of appeal the
matter of whether or not Justice Fraser erred by refusing her request to
adjourn the summary judgment motion, which appears to have been combined with
D.M.’s argument that there were genuine issues requiring a trial.

[240]

Whether to grant or refuse an adjournment of a hearing is a matter of judicial
discretion.
[79]

Factors for a court to consider in deciding to grant or refuse an adjournment,
include: (a) the overall objective of a determination of the matter on its
substantive merits; (b) the principles of natural justice; (c) that justice not
only be done but appear to be done; (d) the particular circumstances of the
request for an adjournment and the reasons and justification for the request; (e)
the practical effect or consequences of an adjournment on both substantive and
procedural justice; (f) the competing interests of the parties in advancing or
delaying the progress of the litigation; (g) the prejudice not compensable in
costs, if any, suffered by a party by the granting or the refusing of the
adjournment; (h) whether the ability of the party requesting the adjournment to
fully and adequately prosecute or defend the proceeding would be significantly
compromised if the adjournment were refused; (i) the need of the administration
of justice to process civil proceedings in an orderly manner; and (j) the need
of the administration of justice to enforce court orders effectively.
[80]
That a party

discretion to grant or refuse an adjournment because a part of the court’s
obligation is to ensure that all litigants have a fair opportunity to advance
their positions.

[241]

review hearing.

[242]

There is no basis for this court to interfere with Justice Fraser’s
decision to proceed with the child protection proceeding. This ground of appeal
fails.

The
doctrine of federal paramountcy provides that when there are valid, but
inconsistent, federal and provincial laws, the federal law prevails and the
provincial law is declared inoperative to the extent of the conflict.
[82]

[252]

However,
the fact that the federal government and a provincial government have
legislated about the same matter does not create a conflict that precludes the
infra
vires
provincial legislation from operating.
[83]
Duplicative
legislation by itself does not raise issues of paramountcy.
[84]
There must be
a conflict for the doctrine of paramountcy to come into effect.

[253]

Two
forms of conflict trigger the doctrine of paramountcy: (1) operational
conflict,

and (2) frustration of purpose.
[85]
Operational
conflict arises when it is impossible to comply with both laws simultaneously.
[86]
Frustration
of purpose arises where although it is possible to comply with both laws, the
operation of the provincial law frustrates the purpose of the federal
enactment.
[87]

[254]

The

that it intended to rule out any possible provincial action in respect of that

conflict in operation as where one enactment says "yes" and the other
says "no"; "the same citizens are being told to do inconsistent

D.M.
seeks to admit over 6,000 pages of fresh evidence and related argument on this

Following
a case management attendance, DM had been directed to file all fresh evidence
material by May 14, 2021. She filed approximately 1,265 pages of fresh evidence
in May. The responding parties carefully reviewed the proposed fresh evidence uploaded
to Caselines in May, consistent with the case management direction. They

reasons for objecting to each of the items the mother seeks to introduce. All

On

hearing, and did not have an opportunity to address the material in their written
submissions.

[274]

This
is not how a child protection appeal can, or should, be argued. Perell, J. has
correctly identified the “legal beacon” of child protection cases: the best
interests of the children.  The court has a duty to ensure that
self-represented litigants receive a fair hearing. The court’s obligations to
self-represented litigants are outlined in the Canadian Judicial Council’s 2006
Statement of Principles on Self-represented Litigants and Accused Persons,
which was endorsed by the Supreme Court in
Pintea v. Johns
,
2017 SCC 23
,
[2017] 1 S.C.R. 470, at para.
4
. The rules which govern the admissibility of
fresh evidence on appeal must be applied with sensitivity to interests of
self-represented litigants. But self-represented litigants must comply with
those rules, and with case management directions. Those rules safeguard the
litigation process in the interests of fairness and justice for all
participants, with respect for the role of the court.

[275]

There
is a statutory provision in the CYFSA which gives priority to updating
information on the child’s best interests. That fresh evidence should be
focused on the best interests of the children. In
L.M
. v. Peel Children's
Aid Society
,
2019 ONCA 841
at para.
84
, the Court of Appeal set out the
framework guiding the admissibility of fresh evidence in child protection
appeals which this court must apply:

[84] Section 121(6) of the CYFSA provides
that the court may receive further evidence relating to events after the
appealed decision. This court has ruled that such fresh evidence should be
admitted in a child protection proceeding if it (a) could not have been adduced
before; (b) is highly relevant in that it provides the court with an accurate
picture of the situation at hand; (c) is potentially decisive to the child's
best interests; (d) is credible; (e) is uncontroverted; and (f) updates
evidence submitted between the time of the prior hearings and the appeal. A
flexible approach [page37] should be taken, given the need for accurate and
up-to-date information concerning the child's best interests…

[276]

In
a recent case, the Court of Appeal noted that when evidence put forward is
"essentially a whole new record, full of lengthy, contextualized
narrative, that expands on issues explored at the trial" it is unlikely to
be admissible as fresh evidence:
Bors v. Bors
,
2021 ONCA 513
at para
59
.
The five affidavits of D.M., with the thousands of pages of attachments, most
of them inadmissible, are essentially an attempt to create a new summary
judgment motion record.

[277]

Perell
J. has identified the frailties of the evidence sought to be adduced. In my
view, none of the evidence sought to be adduced on the appeal meets the
criteria for the admission for fresh evidence set out in section 121(6)  of the
CYFSA, or the more flexible
Palmer
test as applied in child protection
appeals. Even applying the “due diligence” criterion liberally, the appellant
has failed to demonstrate that the evidence is highly relevant, provides an
accurate picture of the situation at hand, is potentially decisive to the
child’s best interests or to an issue decided below, or is credible.

[278]

I
also note that in child protection cases, attempts to introduce voluminous inadmissible
evidence on appeal for the first time is an unwarranted burden on the resources
of the parties and the court. It is not fair to the other parties. Here, the
panel spent days reviewing thousands of additional pages on a half-day appeal.
It inevitably causes significant delay in what is meant to be the expeditious
hearing of child protection appeals, which are given priority by this court.

[279]

I
would dismiss the motion to admit fresh evidence. I agree with the disposition
of the appeal, for the reasons given by Perell J.

[280]

As
the respondents were entirely successful on the appeal, I would award costs to
the respondent father of $18,000, inclusive. He was forced to respond to the
appeal and to the fresh evidence motion. This is an amount which I find to be
reasonable and proportionate in the circumstances. Neither of the other
respondents sought costs, and none are awarded.
